title: You Feel Yourself Decide to Move, Yet Your Brain Starts 350 Milliseconds Earlier

acts.name: 350-Millisecond Brain Lead Paradox & 1983 UCSF Clock Lab
sentences: You feel in charge moving your wrist, yet brain cells fire first!
Yet one fast clock proved your cortex warms up before you choose!
Doctors first saw this in Benjamin Libet's wrist study.
Total nightmare with common sense in nineteen eighty-three.
Libet wired sensors onto testers.
They flicked a wrist when an urge struck.
How do you time when a thought appears?
Subjects watched a green dot circle a scope.
It spun twenty-five times faster than clocks — here is what went wrong.

acts.name: -550ms Readiness Potential vs -200ms Conscious Urge
sentences: Testers logged the dot spot when urges hit.
Wires marked the flick at zero milliseconds, like a finish line.
People felt the urge two hundred milliseconds early, like a shutter.
That seemed normal: thought first, then action.
Then Libet checked waves across forty flicks, like forty sprints.
Above the premotor cortex, the action planner, voltage climbed earlier!
Waves rose at five hundred fifty milliseconds, like a lead!
Your brain prepared three hundred fifty milliseconds early, like a sprinter jumping!
Riding inside your skull was a total nightmare.

acts.name: Kornhuber's 1965 Wave & The 'Free Will Is Dead' Media Panic
sentences: Does that wave mean free will is a lie?
Scientists spotted that wave in nineteen sixty-five.
They called that voltage the Readiness Potential.
Libet's nineteen eighty-three clock proved the wave beat sense!
Critics claimed circuits pull our strings like marionettes.
If your brain decides first, why feel in charge?
Libet searched that final tiny gap.
Flick urges left one hundred fifty milliseconds, like a blink.
But here's the twist: what could your mind do in that gap?

acts.name: Libet's Conscious Veto ('Free Won't') vs Deterministic Myth
sentences: One hundred fifty milliseconds matches a blink.
Libet checked if testers could stop urges.
When subjects vetoed a flick, the wave dropped flat!
Your prefrontal cortex, your brake, slammed shut!
Urges pop up, yet you hold the veto!
In two thousand twelve, Schurger tested that wave.
Was that five hundred fifty millisecond ramp, like a fuse, a choice?
Or had scientists misread random static in the brain?

acts.name: 2012 Schurger Stochastic Noise Accumulator Climax
sentences: Brain waves rise and fall like ocean waves.
When you wait to flick, a crest nudges you over!
Averaging forty trials made crests look like a ramp, like stacked waves!
Instead of a boss, waves rolled like tide!
In two thousand twelve, models matched Libet's curve using noise!
When choices matter, planning leads the motor cortex, your movement strip!
The data shocked the entire lab.
Random flicks never disproved human duty.

acts.name: Using Your 150ms 'Free Won't' Brake in Daily Life & Viewer Takeaway
sentences: How can you use Libet's veto window today?
Ever feel an urge to snap or grab candy?
That urge bubbles up from noisy background waves.
First sparks pop up on cue.
Yet you hold a one hundred fifty millisecond brake, like a pedal!
One slow breath lets your frontal brake cancel the urge.
Freedom lives in the pause between urge and action.
That quiet circuit is why free will acts as a fast brake.

full_script: You feel in control when you flick your wrist, yet your brain fires first! Yet one clock test proved your cortex revs up before you decide! doctors first saw this in Benjamin Libet's Free Will Experiment. Total nightmare with common sense in nineteen eighty-three. In San Francisco, Libet wired sensors onto volunteers. They flicked a wrist whenever an urge struck. How do you time when a thought appears? Subjects watched a green dot circle a scope. It spun twenty-five times faster than a clock — and that wasn't the strangest part. Each person noted where the dot stood when the urge struck. Wires marked the flick at zero milliseconds, like a finish line. People felt the urge two hundred milliseconds early, like a shutter. That seemed normal: thought first, then action. Then Libet checked waves across forty flicks, like forty sprints. Above the premotor cortex, the action planner, voltage climbed earlier! The wave ramped up at five hundred fifty milliseconds, like a lead! Your brain prepared three hundred fifty milliseconds early, like a sprinter jumping! Feeling like a passenger in your skull was a total nightmare. Does that early wave mean free will is a lie? Scientists spotted that wave in nineteen sixty-five. They called that voltage the Readiness Potential. Libet's nineteen eighty-three clock proved the wave beat awareness! Critics claimed circuits pull our strings like marionettes. If your brain decides first, why feel in charge? Libet hated that claim and searched the final gap. Between urge and flick sat a one hundred fifty millisecond window, like a blink. But here's the twist: what could your mind do in that gap? One hundred fifty milliseconds is barely an eye blink. Yet Libet tested if people could cancel an urge. When subjects vetoed a flick, the wave dropped flat! Your prefrontal cortex, the brake behind the forehead, slammed shut! You might not spark every urge, yet you hold the veto! In two thousand twelve, Schurger tested that wave. Was that five hundred fifty millisecond ramp, like a fuse, a choice? Or had scientists misread random static in the brain? Brain waves rise and fall like ocean waves. When you wait to flick, a crest nudges you over! Averaging forty trials made crests look like a ramp, like stacked waves! Instead of a puppeteer, the wave was rolling tide! In two thousand twelve, models matched Libet's curve using noise! When choices matter, planning leads the motor cortex, your movement strip! The data shocked the entire lab Random flicks never disproved human responsibility. How can you use Libet's veto window today? Ever feel an urge to snap or grab candy? That urge bubbles up from noisy background waves. You cannot stop the first spark from popping up. Yet you own the one hundred fifty millisecond brake, like a brake pedal! One slow breath lets your frontal brake cancel the urge. Freedom lives in the pause between urge and action. In everyday life, that means you are not your first impulse, but the gatekeeper who chooses.
